n: Isaiah 36–39 shifts from poetry to history, closely matching 2 Kings 18–20. In 701 BC, Assyria’s King Sennacherib invaded Judah and captured its fortified cities. His own records boast of taking 46 walled towns and shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage.”

f.w: the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah

n: From Lachish, a major Judean city he was besieging, Sennacherib sent his field commander with a large army to Jerusalem. He stood at the same water channel where Isaiah had once met King Ahaz.

f.g: An Assyrian title — “chief cupbearer” or chief officer — not a personal name.
Judah’s second city; Assyrian palace carvings in Nineveh depict its siege.

f.w: the conduit of the upper pool

n: Three of Hezekiah’s officials came out to meet him: Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the secretary, and Joah the record keeper.
The Rabshakeh began his speech: “Tell Hezekiah that the great king of Assyria asks: what are you trusting in?” The question of trust is the theme of the whole confrontation.

f.g: A standard title of Assyrian emperors.

n: “You claim to have strategy and military strength, but those are empty words. Whom are you relying on, that you dare rebel against me?” Hezekiah had stopped paying tribute to Assyria.
“You’re relying on Egypt, that splintered reed! Lean on it and it will pierce your hand.” Ironically, Isaiah had given the same warning about Egypt.

f.w: the staff of this broken reed

n: “And if you say you trust the Lord — didn’t Hezekiah tear down His shrines and altars?” The Assyrian misunderstood: Hezekiah’s reforms removed unlawful hilltop shrines to center worship at the temple.

f.w: whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away

n: He mocks: “Make a bet with my master — I’ll give you two thousand horses if you can even find riders for them!” Judah’s army was tiny compared to Assyria’s.
“How can you repel even the lowest of my master’s officers, relying on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?”
Then a bold claim: “Have I come without the Lord’s approval? The Lord told me to attack this land!” It was propaganda, though Isaiah had said God would use Assyria as His rod (10:5).
Hezekiah’s officials asked him to speak in Aramaic, the diplomatic language they understood, not in Hebrew where the people on the wall could hear and lose heart.

f.g: Aramaic — the international language of diplomacy in that era.

n: He refused crudely: his message was for the ordinary people on the wall, who would soon be reduced to eating and drinking their own waste in a siege. He wanted to break their morale.

f.w: the men that sit upon the wall
f.g: The ordinary soldiers and citizens on the city wall.

n: So the Rabshakeh stood and shouted in Hebrew: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!”
“Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you; he can’t save you.”
“Don’t let him persuade you to trust the Lord, promising that the city won’t fall to Assyria.” The enemy attacks faith itself.

f.w: The LORD will surely deliver us

n: “Don’t listen to Hezekiah. Make peace with me and surrender; then each of you can enjoy your own vine, fig tree, and well.” He uses Israel’s traditional picture of peace as bait.

f.w: every one of his vine, and every one of his fig tree
Make an agreement with me by a present

n: “Until I come and deport you to a land like your own, full of grain, wine, bread, and vineyards.” He makes exile — Assyria’s standard policy — sound pleasant.

f.w: take you away to a land like your own land

n: “Don’t believe Hezekiah when he says the Lord will rescue you. Has any nation’s god saved its land from Assyria?” He puts the Lord on the same level as idols — a fatal mistake.

f.w: Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land

n: “Where are the gods of Hamath, Arpad, and Sepharvaim? Did they save Samaria from me?” All these cities had fallen to Assyria.

f.g: A city whose people Assyria resettled in Samaria (2 Kings 17:24).

n: “Which god of all these lands has ever saved his country from me? So how could the Lord save Jerusalem?” His boast sets up the Lord’s dramatic answer in chapter 37.

f.w: that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem

n: The people stayed silent and didn’t answer, because King Hezekiah had ordered, “Do not answer him.” Silence was wiser than arguing with a mocker.
Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn in grief and reported the Rabshakeh’s words. Chapter 37 tells how Hezekiah turned to the Lord and Isaiah.

f.g: Tearing one’s clothes was a sign of grief or horror at blasphemy.

f.w: told him the words of Rabshakeh
